title: Bharathiraja Took Tamil Cinema Out of the Studio and Into the Soil. He Died at 84, and an Entire Industry Wept.
excerpt: The Padma Shri director who launched Rajinikanth, made Kamal ugly, turned Sridevi into a star, and rewrote the grammar of Indian cinema passed away in Chennai. Chief Minister Vijay declared full state honours.
body:
Before **Bharathiraja**, Tamil cinema largely lived inside studios — polished, urban, stage-lit. After him, it breathed the dust of village roads, smelled of jasmine and rain-soaked earth, and spoke in dialects that Madras had never bothered to learn. When he died on June 10 in Chennai at the age of 84, after months of declining health, it wasn't just a filmmaker the industry lost. It was the man who taught an entire language's cinema how to look at itself honestly.

They called him *Iyakkunar Imayam* — the Himalaya of Directors. It sounds like hyperbole until you look at the filmography.

**16 Vayathinile** (1977), his debut, won the State Award for Best Direction. It featured a young **Kamal Haasan** in a deglamorized role — awkward, ungainly, nothing like the leading man he was becoming — and a luminous **Sridevi** in one of her earliest Tamil performances, a village girl navigating desire and danger with a ferocity that announced a generational talent. **Rajinikanth** played the villain, menacing and magnetic. Three careers launched in a single film, and Bharathiraja directed all of it at 35.

What followed was a decade that rewrote the rules. **Sigappu Rojakkal** (1978) was a psychological thriller about a serial killer — Kamal Haasan, again, this time genuinely terrifying — decades before Tamil cinema had a vocabulary for that kind of darkness. **Kizhakke Pogum Rail** (1978) was pure rural romance, scored by **Ilaiyaraaja** at the peak of his melodic genius. **Tik Tik Tik** (1981) became India's first spy thriller. Each film expanded what Tamil cinema was allowed to be.

> "A lot of films come and go, but his films are timeless. He is great and lives forever." — Director Shankar

The partnership with Ilaiyaraaja deserves its own mythology. Together, they created a sonic landscape for rural Tamil Nadu that didn't exist before — the sound of temple bells dissolving into a lovers' whisper, of train whistles carrying the weight of separation. If you grew up in a Tamil household anywhere in the world, these sounds are in your blood whether you know the films or not.

Actress **Revathi**, whom Bharathiraja introduced to cinema, posted on Instagram: "RIP Bharathiraja Sir — the reason that I am here as an Actor and did the films I did." That sentence carries more weight than any obituary. He didn't just cast actors — he *invented* them. He saw something in people that they hadn't yet seen in themselves, and he built entire films around that discovery.

His health had been failing since the death of his son **Manoj Bharathiraja** — himself an actor-director — in March 2025 at the age of 48. Those close to him said the loss broke something fundamental in the old man, and the months that followed were a slow, grief-shadowed decline.

The tributes that poured in on June 10 read like a roll call of Indian cinema's aristocracy. **Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay** — himself a former film star who understood exactly what Bharathiraja meant to the industry — visited the director's Neelangarai residence in person and announced full state honours. **Rajinikanth**, who owed his early career partly to that villainous turn in *16 Vayathinile*, came to pay his respects. **Suriya**, **Chiranjeevi**, **Pawan Kalyan**, **Mohanlal** — every generation, every language, every corner of South Indian cinema sent its condolences.

**Chiranjeevi** wrote on X: "Indian cinema has lost one of its greatest storytellers." **Khushboo Sundar** called it an "irreplaceable loss." Director **Shankar** said his films were timeless. **Gautami Tadimalla** described him as having "defined an era of Tamil cinema with his timeless classics."

For the diaspora, Bharathiraja holds a particular kind of significance. His films were among the first to be circulated on VHS tapes in the Tamil communities of Singapore, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, the UK, and North America during the 1980s and 90s. For a generation of NRIs who left Tamil Nadu before the digital revolution, his rural landscapes were their last, most vivid image of home — preserved in amber, scored by Ilaiyaraaja, and heartbreakingly beautiful.

His later work included *Karuthamma* (1994) and a segment for Amazon Prime Video's *Modern Love* anthology, proving that even in his seventies and eighties, the instinct for intimate, emotionally precise storytelling never left.

Bharathiraja was a Padma Shri recipient and the founder and president of the Tamil Film Active Producers' Association. He hailed from Theni, in Tamil Nadu's southern hinterland — the same kind of landscape he spent his life putting on screen.

He took the soil of Tamil Nadu, made it cinematic, and gave it back to the world. The screen will look different without him. Smaller, somehow. Less honest.
